opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I think about a lot, because it changes how you allocate effort as a research organization.

For a long time, the bottleneck in research has been human attention. You have a fixed number of really talented researchers, and every bet you make is a bet on where to point that scarce resource. So you end up fairly conservative. You pursue the directions with the clearest signal and the best chance of paying off, and a lot of interesting ideas just never get explored because nobody has the bandwidth.

As models get better at the actual mechanics of research, like writing experiment code, running ablations, reading results, and proposing the next step, that constraint loosens. The cost of trying an idea drops dramatically. And I think that makes the portfolio question more interesting, not less. You can afford many more speculative bets, because the marginal exploration is cheap. The human role shifts toward taste: picking which questions matter, noticing when a result is surprising in a meaningful way versus just noisy, and deciding when to double down.

I'd add a few caveats, though. First, "self-sustaining" is a spectrum. Today models are very useful accelerants on well-scoped sub-problems, but the long-horizon judgment, knowing that a whole line of work is a dead end or that the benchmark you're optimizing is subtly wrong, is still where humans add a lot. Second, compute doesn't disappear as a constraint. If automated research means running far more experiments, you're bottlenecked on GPUs instead of people, so prioritization still matters. It just moves.

And third, the big bets I'm most excited about are the ones that only make sense in this world, where the research process itself becomes the object you're improving. If you can make the loop of hypothesis, experiment, and analysis faster and more reliable, that compounds across everything else. So to me the biggest opportunity isn't any single new direction. It's investing in the infrastructure, evaluation, and safety work that lets you trust a much larger volume of automated research, because that's what unlocks everything downstream.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how stronger research models could change the economics and priorities of research, but it does not argue that the window for major bets before self-sustaining research is small.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because it changes what "a research bet" even means.

Historically, a big bet was expensive mostly in people. You'd take some of your best researchers, point them at something speculative like, say, a totally different architecture or a new training paradigm, and you'd accept that you were pulling them off the main line for a year or two with maybe a twenty percent chance of payoff. The scarce resource was researcher attention. So you had to be very selective, and honestly, a lot of good ideas just never got tried because nobody could justify the headcount.

What's changing is that models are starting to be able to carry a lot of that load themselves. Not all of it yet, but a surprising amount. They can go read everything, reproduce prior results, propose variants, run the experiments, look at the loss curves and say "this didn't work, here's my guess why, here's the next thing to try." When that loop gets reliable enough, the cost of a bet shifts from people to compute. And compute is something you can actually allocate a lot more fluidly than people.

So I think the first-order effect is that you can run way more bets in parallel. Things that would have been a tenth of a person's time become real projects. That's exciting, and I think it means the exploration frontier gets a lot wider.

But there are two places where I'd push back on the fully rosy version. One is that the hard part of research was never really running the experiments. It was picking the question. The taste to say "this is the thing that matters, and this is the thing that's a distraction" is still, in my experience, where the leverage is. Models are getting better at that, but it's also the part where they're most likely to confidently optimize the wrong metric for a long time if you don't check in. So I think the human role moves up a level. You're less of an experimentalist and more of an advisor running a very large, very fast lab.

The second thing is that when experiments are cheap, you get a lot of noise. You'll have a hundred results coming back and some of them will look great for reasons that don't generalize. So the bottleneck becomes evaluation and judgment, figuring out which signals are real. I actually think the organizations that win here are the ones that invest in that layer, in the infrastructure to tell real progress from a lucky seed, rather than just the ones that spin up the most agents.

And then the last piece, which is maybe the most interesting, is that this is a self-reinforcing thing. The bets that improve the model's ability to do research are the highest-leverage bets you can make, because they compound into every other bet. So if you ask me where I'd put the chips, it's less on any particular capability and more on closing that loop, making the model a better scientist. That's the bet that makes all the other bets cheaper.

r001.rationale: The response discusses models increasingly carrying out research and how that could change research bets, but it does not argue that the remaining window for major bets is small.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a really interesting moment, because there are two questions that get bundled together. One is: can you get a model to do useful research work? The other is: can it sustain a research agenda—choose a good problem, run experiments, interpret the results, and decide what to try next? That second thing is a much higher bar.

And I don’t think approaching that bar means we’re running out of room for big research bets. It potentially makes those bets more accessible. If experiments become cheaper and you can explore more ideas, you can take a chance on directions that would have been too expensive to pursue before.

The bottleneck then shifts toward judgment. What’s actually worth investigating? How do you distinguish a result that looks promising from one that changes your understanding? How do you give the system feedback that rewards real progress?

So I’d want a portfolio: keep improving the capabilities that make research assistance useful today, but also leave room for ideas with a longer payoff. The exciting possibility is that better models don’t just help us execute the research agenda we already have. They help us discover questions we wouldn’t have thought to ask.

r001.rationale: The response says approaching self-sustaining research does not mean we are running out of room for major bets; it may make them more accessible. It does not argue the remaining window is small.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a really exciting time to make those bets. As models get better at doing research, the cost of exploring an idea could come down dramatically. You can try more things, get feedback faster, and pursue directions that would otherwise require a huge investment of researcher time.

But I don’t think that makes choosing the direction less important. There’s a difference between a model that can run experiments and a model that can identify a genuinely important problem, question the assumptions behind it, and keep making progress when the obvious approaches fail. That’s a much higher bar for self-sustaining research.

So I’d think about it in two parts: what are the research bets that could unlock that capability, and what would you want to explore once you have it? You want to invest in both. And you want the ability to evaluate the work to improve alongside the ability to produce it, because generating more experiments is only useful if you can tell which results to trust.

r001.rationale: The response discusses opportunities for research bets as models improve, but it does not say the remaining window to make those bets is small.
